text:
Self-Serving Message

This is the tale of a kindly Rabbi, his sweet daughter and the cat who loves her. The tale seems promising at first, until it delves into bitterness over God and those who love Him and follow His laws. The cat represents the glorification of sin itself, and delights whenever the book's characters fall into ungodly habits, judging them forever as hypocrites (taking no account into repentance and future avoidance of said sin). As is the case with most humanist literature the story down spirals from that point until it ends with the Rabbi losing faith in God. At this point the cat is truly happy with the Rabbi, thus giving the tale a 'happy ending'. In short, 'The Rabbi's Cat' is a tale structured to appeal to secular humanists, atheists and pagans who want to feel better about their self-serving, do as you feel, lifestyles.One more note: This book, despite the beautiful artwork and appealing cover, is definitely not appropriate for children.

I recently decided to give the game another chance, hoping years of updates had addressed those problems.

Instead, I found that nearly everything about the game feels like trying to run a footrace underwater.

Engineering is still effectively mandatory if you want to participate in combat without being hopelessly outclassed. The catch? To get the materials needed for engineering, you're often pushed into fighting enemies who are already engineered while you have none of the upgrades yourself. text:
[h1]Better Than Launch, But Still Falls Short[/h1]

Starfield is a much better game in 2026 than it was at launch. The patches have improved the experience, and I had a good time overall.

That said, Shattered Space was disappointing. I eventually left the DLC and went back to exploring the galaxy because I was having more fun doing random things than playing the expansion.

The NG+ system is an interesting idea, but it never feels fully realized. There is also a lot of repetition, and the game still doesn't have the depth of mod support that Skyrim had at a similar point in its life.

On the positive side, ship building is very fun. I also enjoyed base building far more than I expected.

One confession: I always make sure my ships have enough toilets so none of the crew has to wait. If that makes me weird... so be it.

Starfield is one of those games that is almost great. It has flashes of brilliance mixed with repetitive systems and unrealized ideas. Despite its flaws, I enjoyed my time with it.

7/10. Worth playing, especially if you can pick it up on sale.

text:
It's kinda pricey for what it is, but it definitely is as advertised. It's a simple mini golf game to play with friends and while it doesn't deliver the most invigorating experience, it's still the kind of simple competition that can be fun with friends.

The mechanics are super simple and easy to learn, and the holes are designed well with each course feeling unique stylistically and gameplay wise. My only real issue with this game is that there isn't a whole lot to it. It is simply a mini golf game to play with friends and it certainly will provide some fun times, but I did find that it quickly ran out of charm and I kinda lost the desire to keep coming back.

Even still I think it was worth the time I spent on it, I just don't play with friends often enough that a game like this would be necessary for me. It's still a fun concept and plays well, so I do recommend it but be warned that it isn't much more than just "Golf With Your Friends". But hey, if you wanna have some fun with friends I do think this is a pretty good option.

An absolute gem in the series, and for Space Games in general. Be prepared for the traditional steep learning curve as usual, but once you get round that, you are in for a treat. Whether you like dogfighting, fleet battles, station building, or trading, X4 will give you what you're looking for.

The devs are on the ball, with big, game-changing updates coming out every year 9-12 months or so. I just wish there were a few more DLCs so we could continue to support them monetarily.

An active mod scene will keep everything fresh for you. New ships, commands, scripts, paint jobs, faction behaviours, border wars, cheat menus, all the way up to entire overhaul mods turning the universe into Star Wars, it'll have whatever you're looking for, either via the Steam Workshop or Nexus (whichever you prefer).

10/10
